clinical_knowledge.topic: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (ruptured aneurysm) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (ruptured aneurysm) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes urgent neurosurgical/endovascular securing of the aneurysm (coiling or clipping), blood pressure control, and Nimodipine to prevent delayed cerebral vasospasm, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden, explosive, instantaneous peak 'worst headache of my life' (thunderclap headache) followed by neck stiffness and photophobia

Key HPI features: 49F presenting with sudden thunderclap headache where non-contrast head CT demonstrates acute subarachnoid blood filling the basal cisterns requiring urgent neurosurgical/endovascular coiling and Nimodipine to prevent delayed vasospasm.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 92, BP 168/96 (reactive hypertension), RR 18, Temp 37.0C, GCS 14 (mildly drowsy, oriented). Nuchal rigidity present with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Photophobia noted; pupils equal and reactive with no focal motor deficit. Hunt and Hess Grade II, Fisher Grade 3. STAT Non-Contrast Head CT demonstrates acute hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures, most pronounced around the anterior communicating artery region. CT Angiography confirms a 7 mm saccular (berry) aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (ruptured aneurysm).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Migraine without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Headache reaching maximal intensity within seconds — the defining feature of a thunderclap headache.
management_principles: Blood pressure control: titrate IV Nicardipine or Labetalol to keep systolic BP <160 mmHg prior to aneurysm securing, avoiding excessive drops that could worsen cerebral perfusion
Administer oral or NG Nimodipine 60 mg q4h starting within 96 hours to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm (does not reduce aneurysm rebleeding risk)

Immediate neurosurgical/neuro-interventional consultation for urgent aneurysm securing via endovascular coiling or surgical clipping, with admission to a Neuro-ICU for frequent neuro checks and seizure prophylaxis
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 49F presenting with a sudden, explosive, instantaneous-peak 'worst headache of my life' (thunderclap headache) followed by neck stiffness and photophobia, classic for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 92, BP 168/96 (reactive hypertension), RR 18, Temp 37.0C, GCS 14 (mildly drowsy, oriented). Nuchal rigidity present with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Photophobia noted; pupils equal and reactive with no focal motor deficit. Hunt and Hess Grade II, Fisher Grade 3. STAT Non-Contrast Head CT demonstrates acute hyperdense blood filling the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures, most pronounced around the anterior communicating artery region. CT Angiography confirms a 7 mm saccular (berry) aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery.
reference_soap.assessment: Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (Hunt and Hess Grade II, Fisher Grade 3) secondary to a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
reference_soap.plan: STAT emergency neurosurgical protocol: 1. Blood pressure control: titrate IV Nicardipine or Labetalol to keep systolic BP <160 mmHg prior to aneurysm securing, avoiding excessive drops that could worsen cerebral perfusion. 2. Administer oral or NG Nimodipine 60 mg q4h starting within 96 hours to reduce the risk of delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm (does not reduce aneurysm rebleeding risk). 3. Immediate neurosurgical/neuro-interventional consultation for urgent aneurysm securing via endovascular coiling or surgical clipping, with admission to a Neuro-ICU for frequent neuro checks and seizure prophylaxis.

learning_objectives: Recognize the classic thunderclap headache presentation (instantaneous peak intensity, 'worst headache of my life') and associated meningismus signs of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage

Understand the diagnostic pathway: non-contrast head CT as first-line, followed by CT angiography (or lumbar puncture for xanthochromia if CT is negative but suspicion remains) to identify the aneurysm
Apply grading scales (Hunt and Hess for clinical severity, Fisher for vasospasm risk) to guide prognosis and monitoring intensity
Explain the rationale for Nimodipine in preventing delayed cerebral ischemia from vasospasm, and the importance of controlled blood pressure lowering before the aneurysm is secured

teaching.one_liner: A ruptured berry aneurysm bleeds into the space around the brain, causing a sudden 'thunderclap' headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds — a true neurosurgical emergency needing urgent imaging and aneurysm securing.
red_flags: Headache reaching maximal intensity within seconds — the defining feature of a thunderclap headache

must_ask.say: Did this headache reach its worst point within seconds, and is it truly the worst headache of your life?
Have you had neck stiffness or sensitivity to light?
Any weakness, vision changes, or loss of consciousness?
What were you doing when the headache started?

history.answer: My head suddenly felt like it was exploding about two hours ago, and it is the worst headache of my entire life.
It hit me all at once in literally two seconds like a lightning bolt, reaching maximum ten out of ten intensity immediately.
It started two hours ago and has not let up at all; I have never had any headache like this before in my life.
The pain is all over my head, but it is especially terrible in the back of my head and spreading down into my neck.
It feels like a sudden explosion or a massive blow to the head, constantly ten out of ten in severity.
It has been nonstop since it struck, and any slight movement of my head or neck makes it agonizingly worse.
No, there were no flashing lights, blind spots, tingling, or warning signs before it hit.
Yes, the pain made me extremely nauseous and I threw up twice right after it started.
Yes, the bright lights in the room hurt my eyes terribly, and loud sounds make my head pound even worse.
No, I have not had any red tearing eyes, runny nose, or drooping eyelids.
I do not feel feverish and have no rash, but my neck has become very stiff and painful to bend.
No, I have not had any weakness in my arms or legs, numbness, slurred speech, or seizures, just drowsiness from the sheer pain.
No double vision or loss of sight, just severe pain when looking at lights.
No, my temples are not tender, and I have no pain in my jaw when chewing or stiffness in my shoulders.
No, I did not hit my head or suffer any fall or injury.
I took two ibuprofen tablets at home about an hour ago, but they did not help at all.
I was lifting a heavy laundry basket and straining when the headache suddenly exploded in my head.
I have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, and I do not take any blood thinners or aspirin.
history.topic: High blood pressure and blood thinners

history.answer: No, nobody else at home has a headache, and we do not use gas space heaters or anything like that.
No, I have never had cancer and I do not have any problems with my immune system.
I thought it was the worst migraine of my life brought on by severe stress at work. I'm terrified I'm having a massive stroke just like the one that killed my grandmother.
I have always been healthy and have no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital except for childbirth years ago.
I do not take any prescription medications, vitamins, or daily supplements.
No, I have no known allergies to any medications.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink a glass of wine once or twice a month, and nothing in the past week.
I work as an office administrator and live with my husband and teenage daughter.
There is no family history of brain aneurysms, strokes, or kidney diseases that I know of.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular, and there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 168/96 mmHg, pulse is 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 37.0°C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
The patient is mildly drowsy but fully oriented to person, place, and time, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14.
Marked nuchal rigidity is present with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Marked photophobia is noted; pupils are equal, round, and briskly reactive to light, with sharp optic disc margins and no papilledema on fundoscopy.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with full extraocular motility, symmetric facial movements, and normal palate elevation.
Normal muscle tone and 5/5 strength throughout all four extremities without pronator drift or focal weakness.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation bilaterally across all four limbs without sensory level or neglect.
Biceps, patellar, and Achilles reflexes are 2+ and symmetric, with down-going plantar reflexes bilaterally.
No tenderness over the frontal or maxillary sinuses, and no tenderness or thickening over the temporal arteries.
